==Early life and education==
Donald was born Athene Margaret Griffith in London, to Walter Griffith and Annette Marian Tylor.<ref name="EP">{{cite book |author=Europa Publications |date=2003 |title=The International Who's Who 2004 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sR4Ch1dMe8IC&q=alan+ewen+donald+son+robert+t+donald&pg=PA443 |publisher=Psychology Press |page=443 |isbn=978-1-8574-3217-6 }}</ref> She was educated at [[Camden School for Girls]]<ref name="whoswho"/> and the [[University of Cambridge]] where she was an undergraduate student of [[Girton College, Cambridge]]. She earned a bachelor's degree in [[Natural Sciences (Cambridge)|Natural Science (Theoretical Physics)]], followed by a PhD in 1977 for research on [[electron microscopy]] of [[grain boundary]] embrittled systems.<ref name="donaldphd">{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|first=Athene|last=Donald|title=Electron microscopy of grain boundary embrittled systems|publisher=University of Cambridge|year=1977|url=https://idiscover.lib.cam.ac.uk/permalink/f/t9gok8/44CAM_ALMA21431234590003606|website=cam.ac.uk|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.453809}}|author-link=Athene Donald|oclc=500427378}}</ref>

==Research and career==
Donald worked at [[Cornell University]] as a [[Postdoctoral research|postdoctoral associate]], where she switched from working on metals to polymers, before returning to Cambridge (Department of Materials Science) in 1981 and to the [[Cavendish Laboratory]] in 1983. She became Professor of Experimental Physics in 1998. Her major domain of study is [[soft matter physics]], particularly its applications to living organisms and the relationship between structure and other properties.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jenkins|first1=P.J.|last2=Cameron|first2=R. E.|last3=Donald|first3=A.M.|author-link3=Athene Donald|doi=10.1002/star.19930451202|title=A Universal Feature in the Structure of Starch Granules from Different Botanical Sources|journal=Starch - Stärke|volume=45|issue=12|page=417|year=1993}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Krebs|first1=M.R.H.|last2=Bromley|first2=E.H.C.|last3=Donald|first3=A.M.|author-link3=Athene Donald|doi=10.1016/j.jsb.2004.08.002|title=The binding of thioflavin-T to amyloid fibrils: Localisation and implications|journal=Journal of Structural Biology|volume=149|issue=1|pages=30–37|year=2005|pmid=15629655}}</ref>

Her research has applied microscopy, and in particular [[environmental scanning electron microscope|environmental scanning electron microscopy]], to the study of both synthetic and biological systems, notably protein aggregation.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Donald|first1=A.M.|author-link1=Athene Donald|last2=Windle|first2=A.H.|last3=Brand|first3=H.R.|doi=10.1063/1.2809100|title=Liquid Crystalline Polymers|journal=Physics Today|volume=46|issue=11|page=87|year=1993|bibcode = 1993PhT....46k..87D |hdl=2060/19900017655|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author1=Windle, A.H. |author2=Donald, A.D. |title=Liquid crystalline polymers|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location=Cambridge, UK|year=1992|isbn=978-0-521-30666-9}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://people.bss.phy.cam.ac.uk/~amd3/|title=Professor Athene Donald|website=people.bss.phy.cam.ac.uk}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Starch: structure and functionality|publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry|location=Cambridge, England|year=1997|isbn=978-0-85404-742-0}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=The importance of polymer science for biological systems: University of York|date=March 2008|publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry|location=Cambridge, England|isbn=978-0-85404-120-6}}<!--|access-date=7 April 2016--></ref>

Further details of her research can be found in the citation for the Faraday Medal she was awarded by the Institute of Physics in 2010:<ref>{{Cite web|title=2010 Faraday medal|url=http://www.iop.org/about/awards/gold/faraday/medallists/page_43950.html|publisher=iop.org|access-date=23 February 2016|first=Institute of|last=Physics|year=2010}}</ref>

{{blockquote|Professor Donald's deeply innovative and productive research is in experimental soft condensed matter physics, incorporating polymer and colloidal physics, and more recently biological physics. Her early Cornell work on glassy polymer crazing remains very influential and was followed by insightful studies of shear deformation in liquid crystal polymers (LCPs).

Here she was able to demonstrate the ubiquity of the so-called banded texture after shear of LCP's and study the underlying packing of the molecules by electron microscopy showing how they followed a serpentine trajectory in several thermotropics. She also carried out important work on lyotropic systems, including a synthetic polypeptide, studying its gelation and phase diagram.

Donald's mid-career launch into biological physics followed naturally from this polymer work leading to the physics of food and thence to starch. The starch granule structure and its changes during different processing histories were brilliantly analysed using a novel X-ray scattering technique. Structural changes during cooking, with the amylopectin molecule imaginatively treated as a side chain liquid crystalline polymer, brought understanding to different processing treatments. The misfolding of proteins forming amyloid fibrils is well recognized in the aetiology of many diseases, particularly those of old age. Donald's recent work has demonstrated that this important and challenging problem can be powerfully addressed by the approaches of polymer science and furthermore suggests an intriguing connection between the structures observed in both fields.

Donald's impressive achievements in biological physics are strongly based on the imaginative use environmental scanning electron microscopy (ESEM), neutron and X-ray scattering, optical microscopy and infrared spectroscopy. With ESEM in particular her success is supported by her many earlier pioneering investigations of its basic physics. To maintain this vital interchange between soft matter physics and biology, Donald has founded a well resourced Biology and Soft Systems (BSS) Group at the Cavendish.}}

===Administrative work===
Donald was a [[Fellow]] of [[Robinson College, Cambridge]] from 1981 to 2014, when she became Master of Churchill College. She was a member of the [[ESPCI|ESPCI ParisTech]] scientific committee during that time.<ref>[http://www.espci.fr/actu/081117_ISC.pdf Profile], ESPCI.fr. Retrieved 6 May 2016. {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081126040128/http://www.espci.fr/actu/081117_ISC.pdf |date=26 November 2008 }}</ref> She is now an honorary fellow of both Robinson College<ref>[https://www.robinson.cam.ac.uk/college-life/academic-life/fellows List of fellows, Robinson College]</ref> and Girton College.

From 2009 to 2014, she was a member of the Council of Cambridge University. She has previously been a member of the Advisory Council of the [[Campaign for Science and Engineering]],<ref name="CaSE Advisory Council">{{cite web|url=http://www.sciencemuseum.org.uk/GSearch?terms=Athene+Donald|title=Athene Donald-related articles|access-date=11 February 2011}}</ref> and was a Trustee of the [[Science Museum Group]] from 2011-16.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.sciencemuseum.org.uk/about_us/press_and_media/press_releases/2011/08/NMSI%20announces%20four%20new%20Trustees.aspx |title=Science Museum press release |access-date=14 November 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111114044359/http://www.sciencemuseum.org.uk/about_us/press_and_media/press_releases/2011/08/NMSI%20announces%20four%20new%20Trustees.aspx |archive-date=14 November 2011 |url-status=dead  }}</ref> She was a member of the Scientific Council of the [[European Research Council]] from 2013-2018.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Scientific Council – ERC: European Research Council|url=https://erc.europa.eu/about-erc/organisation-and-working-groups/scientific-council|publisher=Europa (web portal)|access-date=23 February 2016|archive-date=20 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160920102530/https://erc.europa.eu/about-erc/organisation-and-working-groups/scientific-council|url-status=dead}}</ref> She chaired the Scientific Advisory Council of the Department of Culture, Media and Sports from 2015 to 2017.{{citation needed|date=May 2020}}

Donald was the first chair of the Institute of Physics biological physics group from 2006 to 2010, and coordinated the writing of lecture notes in biological physics.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Biological Physics |url=http://biologicalphysics.iop.org |website=biologicalphysics.iop.org |access-date=23 February 2016}}</ref> From 2006 to 2008, from 2012 to 2015, and 2021-2024, she served on the Council of the [[Royal Society]], and from 2010 to 2014 she chaired their education committee. She is currently very involved with their policy work, including around skills. For 2015–16, she was President of the [[British Science Association]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Athene Donald announced as next President of the BSA|date=16 February 2015 |url=http://www.britishscienceassociation.org/News/athene-donald-announcement|publisher=britishscienceassociation.org|access-date=23 February 2016}}</ref> She chaired the Interdisciplinary Advisory Panel for REF2021.

As Master of Churchill College, in June 2021 Donald was involved in a dispute regarding the College's Working Group on Churchill, Race, and Empire.<ref>{{cite news|last=Adams|first=Richard|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2021/jun/17/cambridge-college-ends-critical-examination-of-founder-winston-churchill|title=Cambridge college ends critical examination of founder Winston Churchill|work=The Guardian|date=17 June 2021|access-date=19 June 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=A Statement from the Master – Churchill College|url=https://www.chu.cam.ac.uk/news/2021/jun/17/statement-master/|access-date=2021-06-23|website=www.chu.cam.ac.uk|date=17 June 2021 }}</ref>

===Diversity work===
Donald has been an outspoken champion of women in science. From 2006 to 2014 she was director of WiSETI, Cambridge University's Women in Science, Engineering and Technology Initiative, and she was the university's first Gender Equality Champion from 2010 to 2014.<sup>[23]</sup> Outside the university, she chaired the [https://people.bss.phy.cam.ac.uk/~amd3/old%20web%20stuff/ATHENAFORUM/ Athena Forum] from 2009 to 2013. She sat on the BIS (later BEIS) Diversity group, and serves the Equality and Diversity Board of [[University of Sheffield|Sheffield University]] and the Gender Balance Working Group of the [[European Research Council|ERC]]; she is a Patron of the [[Daphne Jackson Trust]]. She regularly writes on the topic of women in science in both mainstream media,<ref>{{Cite news|title = Just one action for women in science|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/occams-corner/2015/jun/19/just-one-action-for-women-in-science|newspaper=The Guardian|date=19 June 2015|access-date=23 February 2016|issn=0261-3077}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title=Girls soar in science, yet why still so few women in the lab?|url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2014/mar/15/women-equal-but-not-treated-equally|newspaper=The Guardian|date=15 March 2014|access-date=23 February 2016|issn=0261-3077}}</ref> and on her personal blog.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://occamstypewriter.org/athenedonald/|title = Athene Donald's Blog}}</ref> She gives many talks on this issue.

She is the author of ''Not Just for the Boys: Why We Need More Women in Science,'' published in 2023.

She was awarded the UKRC's Lifetime Achievement Award in 2011,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Professor Dame Athene Donald receives Lifetime Achievement Award|url=http://www.iop.org/news/11/may/page_50837.html|publisher=iop.org|access-date=23 February 2016|first=Institute of|last=Physics}}</ref> a Suffrage Science award by the [[Medical Research Council (United Kingdom)|MRC]] in 2013<ref>{{Cite web|title=Suffrage Science 2013 Events – MRC Clinical Sciences Centre|url=http://csc.mrc.ac.uk/suffrage-science-2013-events|website=csc.mrc.ac.uk|access-date=23 February 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151024063731/http://csc.mrc.ac.uk/suffrage-science-2013-events/|archive-date=24 October 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> and her portrait by Tess Barnes hangs in the Cavendish Laboratory.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Should I Be Discombobulated?|url=http://occamstypewriter.org/athenedonald/2014/12/12/should-i-be-discombobulated|website=Athene Donald blogsite|access-date=23 February 2016}}</ref> Donald talks about some of the issues for women in science in this video.

===Awards and honours===
In 1999 Donald was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS).<ref name=frs>[http://royalsociety.org/people/athene-donald Royal Society profile]</ref> Her nomination reads:<ref name="royal"/>

{{blockquote|Athene Donald is distinguished for her work relating mechanical properties to the structure of [[polymer]]s. She showed that polymer [[crazing]] could not be understood without reference to the [[Reptation|entanglement network]], and showed that two processes are involved, chain scission and chain disentanglement, depending differently on temperature and [[molecular weight]]. This work underpins the understanding of [[brittleness]] and [[ductility]] in solid polymers. She pioneered studies of [[Thermotropic crystal|thermotropic]] [[liquid crystal]]line polymers via [[transmission electron microscopy]], revealing the ubiquity of banded textures after [[shear flow]] in these materials. More recently, she has developed [[X-ray]] methods for characterising [[starch]], thereby opening up the field to novel physical methods which enhance those of the [[botany|plant biologists]] and [[food science|food scientists]].}}

*2019: Lifetime Achievement Award from [[Times Higher Education|THE]].<ref>{{Cite web|title = Times Higher Education Awards 2019: winners announced|url=https://www.timeshighereducation.com/news/times-higher-education-awards-2019-winners-announced|access-date=29 November 2019|date=28 November 2019}}</ref>
*2021: Honorary Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]].<ref>{{Cite web|title = Honorary Fellows at the Royal Society of Chemistry|url=https://www.rsc.org/about-us/our-history/our-honorary-fellows|access-date=1 September 2023|date=1 September 2023}}</ref>

{{div col end}}

==Personal life==
Donald has been married to [[mathematician]] Matthew J. Donald since 1976;<ref name="EP"/><ref name="whoswho"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bss.phy.cam.ac.uk/~mjd1014|title=A Many-Minds Interpretation of Quantum Theory|publisher=University of Cambridge|access-date=31 December 2013|archive-date=3 January 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140103071751/http://www.bss.phy.cam.ac.uk/~mjd1014/|url-status=dead}}</ref> the couple have two children, a son and a daughter,<ref name="EP"/><ref name="DIDiscs AD"/> and two grandchildren.
